title: Companion animal practice group: pragmatic trial of a nurse-led weight clinic for overweight dogs with osteoarthritis

inputs.need:
I am the clinical director of a group of 12 first-opinion companion animal practices. Osteoarthritis is one of the most common reasons older dogs are brought to us, and most of these dogs are overweight. At the moment our vets give weight advice and a diet leaflet during the consultation and prescribe pain relief, but very few owners come back for weight checks, and we rarely see the weight loss we recommend.

Two of our practices have run a nurse-led weight clinic for a year: monthly weigh-ins with a registered veterinary nurse, a measured daily food allowance with a therapeutic diet, a written exercise plan, and a phone check-in between visits. The nurses and owners like it, and our board is asking whether to roll it out to all 12 practices. Before we do, I want a pragmatic trial comparing the nurse-led clinic with usual vet-led advice for overweight dogs with osteoarthritis, run in everyday practice with our own staff and the owners who come through the door.

What matters to owners is how comfortably their dog moves, so I think the main outcome should be the owner-completed mobility score we already use (the Canine Mobility and Comfort Index, 11 items), with body weight, lameness assessed by a vet who does not know the group, pain relief use and whether owners stay with the program as other outcomes. We would enrol for about six months and follow each dog for six months. We have no external funding; the group covers nurse time and a discounted diet. I need help with how to allocate dogs, how many we need, how to limit bias when owners know which group they are in, and the ethics path for a study in client-owned animals.
inputs.constraints: No external funding; the practice group covers nurse time and a discounted therapeutic diet. Enrolment must fit normal consultation times, and each practice can run at most two weight clinic sessions a week. Dogs in the usual-care group cannot be asked to attend extra visits beyond a six-month review.
localFacts: The practice group's clinical research ethics committee for client-owned animals approved the protocol on 2026-09-02 (CREC-2026-022), with written owner consent.
The group's board approved nurse time for up to two weight clinic sessions a week in each practice from November 2026 (board minute PG-2026-37).
Across the 12 practices, about 45 overweight dogs with a new or existing osteoarthritis diagnosis are seen each month.
The diet manufacturer offers the therapeutic diet at a 40 percent discount to enrolled dogs in both groups and has no role in the study (letter DM-2026-17).
Two practices have run the nurse-led weight clinic since September 2025; 61 dogs attended at least one weigh-in.

records.title: Weight reduction and owner-reported mobility in overweight dogs with osteoarthritis: a randomised trial in referral practice
records.authors: Hallorann-Ueda P, Brightwell-Osei A, Fonseca-Lind M
records.abstract: Sixty-two overweight dogs with osteoarthritis at a referral hospital were randomly allocated to a supervised weight loss programme or to diet advice alone for 16 weeks. Dogs in the programme lost a median of 9.4 percent of body weight against 2.1 percent. Owner-reported mobility scores improved by a mean of 6.1 points on a 44-point index in the programme group and by 1.8 points with advice alone. Lameness assessed on a force plate improved in dogs that lost at least 6 percent of body weight. Owners were not blinded, and referral patients may be more motivated than first-opinion clients.

records.title: Nurse-led weight clinics in first-opinion practice: attendance and weight outcomes in 1,240 dogs
records.abstract: We reviewed attendance and weight records for 1,240 dogs enrolled in nurse-led weight clinics at 31 first-opinion practices. Only 38 percent of dogs attended for six months. Among dogs that completed six months, median weight loss was 8.1 percent, and 44 percent lost at least 10 percent of their starting weight. Dogs whose owners received a phone call between visits were more likely to keep attending. Outcomes for dogs that stopped attending were unknown, so average weight loss across all enrolled dogs could not be estimated.

records.title: Validation of an owner-completed mobility and comfort index for dogs with chronic joint pain
records.authors: Ogunleye-Harper S, Vitale-Kristensen E, Moss-Achebe D
records.abstract: We evaluated an 11-item owner-completed index of mobility and comfort, scored 0 to 44 with higher scores meaning worse, in 212 dogs with chronic joint pain and 80 healthy dogs. Internal consistency was 0.91 and test-retest reliability over one week was 0.88. Scores were higher in dogs with more severe radiographic osteoarthritis and fell after pain relief was started. Owners' judgements of meaningful change corresponded to a difference of about 4 points. The standard deviation of change scores was 8 points. The index was validated with English-speaking owners only.

records.title: Activity monitor counts versus owner-reported mobility in dogs with osteoarthritis
records.abstract: Forty-eight dogs with osteoarthritis wore a collar-mounted activity monitor for two weeks before and after the start of pain relief, while their owners completed a mobility index. Changes in activity counts correlated only moderately with changes in owner scores (correlation 0.41). When dogs received an inactive tablet during a blinded phase, owners still reported improvement of about 2 points, suggesting a caregiver expectation effect. The authors suggest that trials with unblinded owners should add an outcome assessed by someone who does not know the allocation.

records.title: Owner adherence to calorie restriction plans for dogs: a prospective study in nine practices
records.authors: Lachance-Obi R, Sundqvist-Mahlangu H, Ferris-Tanaka O
records.abstract: We followed 310 dogs started on a calorie restriction plan in nine first-opinion practices for six months. Owners reported following the daily food allowance on 81 percent of days in the first month and on 57 percent of days in the sixth month. Begging, scavenging or waking at night for food were reported by 34 percent of owners, and these dogs lost less weight. Households with children or several adults feeding the dog had lower adherence. The authors recommend asking about hunger behaviours at every visit.

records.title: Pragmatic trials in companion animal practice: recruitment and retention across practice groups
records.abstract: We summarised recruitment and retention in 14 pragmatic trials run in first-opinion practice groups. Median recruitment was 3.2 animals per practice per month, ranging from 0.8 to 6.1, and was highest where a named nurse or vet champion screened appointment lists. Median retention at six months was 78 percent. Trials that allocated animals centrally by a web system reported fewer protocol deviations than those using envelopes held in practices. Outcome assessment by a clinician unaware of allocation was reported in 6 of 14 trials.

records.title: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory use during weight loss programmes in dogs with osteoarthritis
records.abstract: We reviewed prescribing records for 205 dogs with osteoarthritis enrolled in weight loss programmes at four practices. Among dogs that lost at least 10 percent of their starting weight, 29 percent had their non-steroidal anti-inflammatory dose reduced or stopped within six months, against 8 percent of dogs that lost less. Dose changes were made by the treating vet without a protocol, and some reductions may have reflected owner preference. The authors suggest recording analgesic use as an outcome in weight loss trials.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. One referral trial found supervised weight loss improved owner-reported mobility by more than the 4-point change owners consider meaningful, but owners were unblinded and owners report improvement even with an inactive tablet. Nurse-led clinics in first-opinion practice lose most dogs before six months, adherence to food allowances falls over time and hunger behaviours are common. Practice-based pragmatic trials recruit about three animals per practice per month and run more cleanly with central allocation. The evidence supports a pragmatic comparison with a blinded secondary outcome and close attention to retention.
response.gradeRationale: One small referral trial with unblinded owners and several observational studies; indirect for first-opinion practice and imprecise.

response.reading: The clinic works through owners: it changes what they feed, how they exercise the dog and whether they come back. Mobility is the outcome owners value, but owners also know which group they are in and report improvement from expectation alone (claim c3), so a blinded lameness assessment and weight are needed alongside. Retention is the weak link of weight clinics (claim c4), and hunger behaviours are the welfare cost to watch. Practice-level differences in nurse enthusiasm call for stratified central allocation (claim c5).

response.rationale: The board needs to know whether the clinic works in its own practices, with its own nurses and ordinary owners, which is an effectiveness question for a pragmatic trial. Individual allocation by a central web system, stratified by practice, keeps the groups comparable and limits deviations (c5). The primary outcome is the owner-reported index, with 4 points as the meaningful difference (c2) and the referral trial as a planning value (c1); because owners report improvement from expectation (c3), lameness is also scored by a vet unaware of allocation. Reporting follows CONSORT with its pragmatic trials extension, and PRECIS-2 documents how pragmatic each domain is.

response.overview: Two-group pragmatic trial in 12 first-opinion practices: dogs are allocated individually 1:1 by a central web system, stratified by practice, to the nurse-led weight clinic or usual vet-led advice, and followed for six months.
response.population: Dogs aged 2 years or older with osteoarthritis diagnosed by a vet, body condition score 7 or more of 9, whose owners give written consent; excluded are dogs with uncontrolled endocrine disease, dogs expected to need joint surgery within six months, and households unable to attend a six-month review.
response.exposure: Clinic group: monthly nurse weigh-ins, measured daily food allowance with the discounted therapeutic diet, written exercise plan and a phone check-in between visits. Usual-care group: vet advice and the diet leaflet at the consultation, the same discounted diet available, and one six-month review.
response.procedures: Vets screen appointment lists weekly; a named nurse champion in each practice approaches owners. After baseline mobility index, weight and a standard lameness video, allocation is obtained from the central web system. At six months every dog, whatever its attendance, has the owner index, weight and a video scored by a vet from another practice who does not know the allocation. Pain relief prescriptions are taken from practice records.

parsimony.simplestPath: Two groups, one owner-reported primary outcome, one blinded secondary outcome, six months.

response.theoreticalFramework: PRECIS-2 to document pragmatism across domains; no behavioural framework beyond the clinic's existing content.
response.summary: Individually allocated pragmatic trial stratified by practice, with one primary, two secondary, one process and one balancing outcome.

response.designSummary: Two-group pragmatic trial, individual allocation stratified by practice; primary analysis by intention to treat.
response.sampleSize: The smallest difference worth detecting is 4 points on the index (claim c2), with a standard deviation of change of 8 points from the validation study. For 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05, 63 dogs per group are needed for an unadjusted comparison; adjusting for the baseline score with an assumed correlation of 0.5 reduces this to about 48 per group. Allowing 20 percent loss to follow-up (retention of 78 percent in practice-based trials) gives 60 per group, 120 dogs, which matches about 20 enrolments a month for six months.
response.primaryAnalysis: Linear regression of six-month index score on group, adjusted for baseline score and practice (stratification factor), by intention to treat; 95 percent confidence interval for the adjusted difference.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Same model for percentage weight change and blinded lameness score; proportion with a pain relief reduction; clinic attendance described; hunger behaviours by group.
response.missingData: Multiple imputation of missing six-month scores using baseline score, practice, age and attendance, with a sensitivity analysis assuming worse outcomes in dogs lost to follow-up.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome; secondary outcomes reported with confidence intervals and not used to claim effectiveness.
response.software: R; statistical analysis plan filed with the ethics committee before the first dog is enrolled.
overfittingGuards: Three adjustment covariates fixed in advance
No subgroup claims beyond a pre-specified practice-size interaction
response.summary: 120 dogs give 80 percent power for a 4-point difference after baseline adjustment and 20 percent loss.

response.risks: Low. Risks for dogs are hunger, too-rapid weight loss and reduced pain relief; nurses follow a maximum weekly loss of 2 percent and any welfare concern is referred to the vet. Owners' risk is inconvenience.
response.consent: Written informed consent from the owner after an information sheet explaining allocation, visits and that usual care continues in either group; owners may withdraw at any time without affecting their dog's care.
response.data: Owner names and addresses stay in practice systems; the trial database holds study numbers, practice and dog data; videos are stored without owner identifiers.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus applied to owners: income (diet discount for both groups), distance from the practice (phone check-ins), age and disability (exercise plans adapted to what owners can do), and language (information sheet in the two most common local languages). Enrolment by practice is monitored so that practices in poorer areas are not under-represented.
response.effectiveness: The trial answers whether the clinic improves mobility enough to justify roll-out; a null result would save nurse time for other care.
response.efficiency: Uses existing nurses, the existing index and one review visit for usual care.
response.costs: Nurse time covered by the group; the diet discount funded by the manufacturer with no role in the study; video scoring by vets within existing time.
response.grants: None needed; a positive result could support a veterinary nursing research award for a cost analysis of roll-out.
response.partnerships: Practice nurse champions, the group board, two owner representatives from the group's client panel, and the diet manufacturer only as a supplier.
response.rebPath: Approved by the practice group's clinical research ethics committee for client-owned animals on 2026-09-02 (CREC-2026-022); welfare stopping rules are part of the approval.
response.limitations: Owners cannot be blinded; six months may be too short for long-term weight maintenance; one practice group.
response.summary: Low-risk trial in client-owned dogs with written owner consent, welfare stopping rules and owner-level equity measures.

response.partnershipPlan: Two owners from the client panel review the information sheet and the hunger-behaviour questions; nurse champions meet monthly with the trial coordinator.
response.socialListening: A three-month read of the group's social media pages and client comments for mentions of weight clinics and diet cost, recorded as composites.

response.title: A nurse-led weight clinic versus usual advice for overweight dogs with osteoarthritis in first-opinion practice: a pragmatic trial
response.abstract: Objective: to compare a nurse-led weight clinic with usual vet-led advice on owner-reported mobility in overweight dogs with osteoarthritis. Design: pragmatic trial in 12 first-opinion practices with individual central allocation stratified by practice. Primary outcome: change in an 11-item owner-reported mobility index at six months. Results will be reported after follow-up.
response.introduction: Excess weight worsens osteoarthritis in dogs, and supervised weight loss improved mobility in a referral trial, but nurse-led clinics in first-opinion practice have not been compared with usual advice, and most dogs stop attending.
response.methods: Dogs with osteoarthritis and a body condition score of 7 or more were allocated 1:1 by a central web system. The primary analysis compares six-month index scores adjusted for baseline and practice by intention to treat; lameness was scored from video by vets unaware of allocation.

store.title: Nurse-led weight clinic versus usual advice for overweight dogs with osteoarthritis in first-opinion practice
store.problem.rawNeed:
I am the clinical director of a group of 12 first-opinion companion animal practices. Osteoarthritis is one of the most common reasons older dogs are brought to us, and most of these dogs are overweight. At the moment our vets give weight advice and a diet leaflet during the consultation and prescribe pain relief, but very few owners come back for weight checks, and we rarely see the weight loss we recommend.

Two of our practices have run a nurse-led weight clinic for a year: monthly weigh-ins with a registered veterinary nurse, a measured daily food allowance with a therapeutic diet, a written exercise plan, and a phone check-in between visits. The nurses and owners like it, and our board is asking whether to roll it out to all 12 practices. Before we do, I want a pragmatic trial comparing the nurse-led clinic with usual vet-led advice for overweight dogs with osteoarthritis, run in everyday practice with our own staff and the owners who come through the door.

What matters to owners is how comfortably their dog moves, so I think the main outcome should be the owner-completed mobility score we already use (the Canine Mobility and Comfort Index, 11 items), with body weight, lameness assessed by a vet who does not know the group, pain relief use and whether owners stay with the program as other outcomes. We would enrol for about six months and follow each dog for six months. We have no external funding; the group covers nurse time and a discounted diet. I need help with how to allocate dogs, how many we need, how to limit bias when owners know which group they are in, and the ethics path for a study in client-owned animals.
